title: Integer Break
description: Brute force to optimized: uncached recursion over every possible split versus the mathematical shortcut of repeatedly breaking off pieces of size 3.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer n, break it into the sum of at least two positive integers, and maximize the product of those integers. Return the maximum product achievable.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","n, an integer at least 2"],["Output","The maximum product of some way of writing n as a sum of at least two positive integers"],["Goal","Find the optimal split without checking every possible partition of n"],["Constraints","2 <= n <= 58"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The best product for n depends on the best product for smaller remainders","Dynamic programming, building up the answer from smaller values"],["A well-known mathematical fact: breaking into parts of size 3 maximizes the product","A direct greedy/mathematical shortcut, once the pattern is recognized"]]}

blocks.text: Split n into two or more positive integers that add up to n, choosing the split that makes their product as large as possible.

blocks.title: Analogy: Cutting a Rope Into Pieces to Maximize the Product of Their Lengths
blocks.text: Picture a rope of length n that must be cut into at least two pieces, and needing to choose the cut points so that multiplying together the lengths of all the pieces gives the largest possible result.

blocks.caption: The best product for n builds on the best products (or raw values) of smaller pieces

blocks.text: The only valid split is 1 + 1, giving a product of 1.
Splitting into 3 + 3 + 4 gives the maximum product, 3 times 3 times 4 = 36.
Before checking every possible way to partition n, notice the best product for n can be built from the best products (or raw values) of smaller pieces.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the first piece cut off has size j, the rest of the rope, of length n minus j, can either be left as one piece OR split further, whichever gives a larger contribution.

Observation 2: This means the best product for n minus j is the LARGER of just leaving it as (n minus j) itself, or the best product from further splitting it, dp[n minus j].

Observation 3: Trying every possible first piece j, and taking the best result, builds dp[n] directly from smaller, already-solved values.

Observation 4: A well-known mathematical fact accelerates this further, breaking a number into pieces of size 3 (with a final piece of 2 or 4 to handle the remainder) always maximizes the product, since 3 is the integer closest to e, the mathematically optimal piece size for this kind of problem.
This leads to two valid strategies: build a dynamic programming table from smaller values upward, or directly apply the "break into 3s" mathematical shortcut once it is recognized.
Recursively try every possible size for the first piece, and recurse on the rest, without caching any results.

items: For a given remaining length, try every possible first piece size from 1 up to that length minus 1.
Recursively find the best product for the remainder, comparing leaving it whole versus splitting it further.
Multiply the first piece by the better of those two options, and take the best result across every choice of first piece.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recursively try every first piece, recomputing shared subproblems

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible first piece is tried, and the remainder is recursively solved from scratch each time.
The same remainder value gets fully re-solved across many different branches of the recursion tree.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential, due to repeated recomputation of overlapping subproblems.
Space: O(n) for the recursion depth.
Limitation: the same remaining length is solved over and over across different branches; caching those results (or recognizing the mathematical shortcut) removes almost all of that repeated work.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recomputing subproblems is wasteful: the best product for a given remaining length never changes no matter how it was reached, so solving it once and reusing that answer is sufficient.

What a bottom-up dp table looks like: dp[i] holds the best product achievable for length i, built from dp values (or raw lengths) at smaller indices.

What the mathematical shortcut reveals: repeatedly breaking off pieces of size 3 (using a final piece of 2 or 4 to cleanly use up the remainder, since breaking further would only hurt) always gives the optimal product, a fact that can replace the dp table entirely once trusted.

The core idea: either build a dp table bottom-up, reusing smaller answers, or directly apply the break-into-3s rule for an O(1) formula-based solution.

Special-case n equal to 2 (answer 1) and n equal to 3 (answer 2), since breaking either further only hurts. For any larger n, repeatedly multiply the running product by 3 and subtract 3 from n, until n is 4 or less, then multiply by whatever remains (which will be 2, 3, or 4).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Running product","n remaining"],"rows":[["Start","1","10"],["Break off a 3","3","7"],["Break off another 3","9","4"],["n is now 4 or less, multiply by the remainder","9 times 4 = 36","done"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: repeatedly break off pieces of size 3, the mathematically optimal piece size

blocks.text: Breaking a number into equal pieces close to the mathematical constant e (approximately 2.718) maximizes the product of the pieces, and among integers, 3 is the closest to e, making it the optimal repeated piece size. Special-casing n of 2 and 3 avoids ever breaking down to a piece of size 1, which always hurts the product (multiplying by 1 never helps), and stopping once 4 or less remains, then using that remainder directly (2, 3, or 4, never further split), completes the optimal breakdown.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one loop breaking off pieces of size 3.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: Integer Break is a case where a dynamic programming solution works, but a direct mathematical insight, breaking into pieces of size 3 (mirroring the constant e) is provably optimal, replaces it entirely with a simple, fast loop.

items: Breaking all the way down to pieces of size 1, which always lowers the product rather than helping it.
Not special-casing n equal to 2 or 3, where the "break into 3s" rule would otherwise force an invalid or suboptimal split.

blocks.text: Mentioning the connection to the mathematical constant e, and why breaking into 3s (over 2s or larger pieces) is provably optimal, demonstrates a deeper understanding than just presenting the dp table.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid a full dp table", think: repeatedly breaking off pieces of size 3 is provably optimal.

items: Can you prove why size-3 pieces beat size-2 pieces for maximizing the product?
How would you solve this with a bottom-up dp table instead, and how does its result compare to the direct formula?
Any "optimal partition size" problem connected to the mathematical constant e.
Dynamic programming problems that can be replaced by a direct greedy/mathematical shortcut once the optimal structure is proven.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in exponential time. The optimized break-into-3s approach runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

items: Pattern: a mathematical optimum (breaking into pieces of size 3) replacing a full dynamic programming table.

Core Idea: repeatedly break off pieces of size 3, since 3 is the integer closest to e, the mathematically optimal piece size for maximizing a product; handle the final remainder (2, 3, or 4) directly.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's recursion, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: breaking into pieces of size 1 always hurts the product; size 3 is provably the best repeated piece size.
Interview Difficulty: the dp version is standard; knowing (or deriving) the size-3 mathematical shortcut is the higher-value insight.
One line memory trick: break into pieces of 3; 3 is closest to e, the optimal piece size.
